In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the circadian clock is a complex molecular system, which is reflected in the complex behaviour of the master clock regulator BMAL1, and which we have been able to quantify in vivo using the Bmal1Vnus mouse model.
the Venus::BMAL mouse model is a valuable resource for understanding the molecular basis of circadian time keeping in the SCN and in peripheral tissues.
the Venus::BMAL fusion protein is a suitable reporter to study circadian rhythms in mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have generated a novel mouse model for live imaging of BMAL1, which has enabled the first quantitative analysis of BMAL1 behaviour in central and peripheral circadian clocks.
Bmal1V Venus mice will provide a powerful resource to investigate the intra cellular mechanisms that regulate the circadian behaviour of the master clock regulator.
we have generated a mouse model that allows us to directly visualise the behaviour of the master circadi an clock regulator BMAL1 in a physiological context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMAL1 is a dynamic protein that cycles in and out of the nucleus in a circadian manner and is subject to circadian control of its molecular abundance.
BMAL1 is not a static, constitutive clock factor but instead undergoes complex, dynamic behaviour that may be a key determinant of its circadian and tissue specific functions.
BMAL1 is expressed in a circadian fashion and is highly mobile between the cytoplasm and nucleus in both central and peripheral tissues.
